newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Prairie crop output a record - CWB analyst.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Prairie crop output a record - CWB analyst.

text.p: Canada's Prairie crop production should reach a record high 52.8 million tonnes for the six major grains, a Canadian Wheat Board analyst said.
That output would exceed last year's western Canadian production of wheat, barley, canola, oats, flax and rye by 14.2 percent, up from 46.2 million tonnes.
"It's the combination of less summerfallow and the shift from oilseeds to higher yielding cereal crops," CWB director of weather and crop surveillance Paul Bullock told an industry briefing here.
The previous largest output was 51 million tonnes in 1986.
Summerfallow was 15 million acres this summer, compared to 24 million acres in 1986, Bullock said.
"Early harvest reports are very positive about quality. The early stuff came off in good shape but the rest is an unknown," Bullock said.

Indications from 150 samples representing about two percent of all western Canada's wheat crop, including durum, suggested protein levels were below last year's early sample, while yields outpaced 1995's early sample by 2.5 percent.
Durum yields were below last year, he added.
"We've got 26 percent harvested by Monday, we've probably got a third done now and we could be at 50 percent by the start of next week," Bullock said.
"There's crop out there that's not ready to be swathed. I'd say 10 percent might still be vulnerable to frost."
Alberta's Peace River Valley and its northern grainbelt in the last eight mornings saw some brief frost with the coldest point in Peace River at -2.8 Celsius, he said.
"Little or nothing's been harvested up there, some swathing was done. We expect to see some damage," he said.
Frost struck Saskatchewan Tuesday and Wednesday mornings with the coldest point at Coronach, near the Montana border, with a low of -3.0 Celsius.
"This is not a deep frost, it maybe lasted an hour," he said.
Diseases and pests were more likely to downgrade the crop.
Fusarium damage in Manitoba and Saskatchewan appeared to be less severe than earlier feared but more ergot was showing up in samples from both provinces, he said.
Wheat midge damage was widespread in northeast and east central Saskatchewan, he said.

"I don't remember a field that didn't have wheat midge in it, but we're finding two or three percent of kernels are affected. We are getting reports of midge damage but it's not a major concern," Bullock said.
"I'd expect more than six percent (off all Prairie wheat output) to grade as feed wheat. The average is 10 percent," he added.
-- Winnipeg bureau 204 947 3548
